meta.note: Years are signed integers (-2500 = 2500 BCE). 'built' = recommended modelled year of completion; 'from' = recommended start of construction; 'to' = recommended end (null = still present, in whatever form, in 1625). Many dimension figures come from Wikipedia pointers and press pages because primary PDFs were not machine-readable; see landscape.md access notes. Wikipedia-derived values are marked in dateNote/unknown where they conflict with other sources.
meta.evidenceEnum: attested-standing | attested-excavated | attested-documentary | attested-pictorial | reconstructed | conjectural

features.name: Robin Hood's Ball causewayed enclosure
features.latLonSource: sto-wp-robinhood (Wikipedia infobox). About 3.8 km N and 2.0 km W of the provisional origin: OUTSIDE the provisional site bounds (z -2800); just outside the northern WHS boundary.

dates.dateNote: Sources disagree: Wikipedia 'probably built c.4000 BC, possibly in use to c.3000 BC'; English Heritage 'centuries around 3500 BC'. No fetched source gives a radiocarbon model. 3600 BCE is the brief's figure. Fell out of use around the time Stonehenge's earliest earthworks began (Wikipedia). Earthwork remained as a low ruin to 1625 (to=null shown in appearance).

dimensions.note: No fetched source gives a diameter or ditch size. Two circuits of ditch with low banks behind; ditch dug in segments.

counts.causewayGaps: one per Wikipedia (other sources say several; unresolved)

appearanceByPeriod.show: Two concentric segmented ditches cut in white chalk, short digs separated by causeways, low fresh chalk banks behind; bare white scars on the hilltop. Inside, little visible (no sources on structures).
Banks and ditch silting, partly grassed; occasional recut/reuse not documented.
Grassed, low rounded ring earthworks on downland; abandoned, no activity attested. A copse NW of it gave the later name; the name Robin Hood's Ball is modern and the 1820 map calls it Neath Barrow.

attested: Causewayed enclosure with two ditch circuits and low banks (sto-wp-robinhood)
Early Neolithic, 'centuries around 3500 BC' (sto-eh-history)
Never comprehensively excavated (sto-wp-robinhood)
Scheduled 1965; within Salisbury Plain Training Area (sto-wp-robinhood)
inferred: Banks were originally fresh white chalk (general causewayed-enclosure practice, not in fetched sources)
Position as a precursor to Stonehenge's landscape (sto-eh-history)
unknown: Whether it lay in clearing or woodland

dates.dateNote: Wikipedia pages conflict: Blick Mead 'continuous habitation c. 8000-4000 BCE'; Vespasian's Camp article 'occupied c. 6250-4700 BCE' (sto-wp-vespasian). Southampton: pollen/DNA cover later Mesolithic (from c. 5500 BC) to Neolithic (c. 4000 BC). Recommend 6250-4000 BCE; low confidence.

appearanceByPeriod.show: A warm spring beside the Avon, hunter-gatherer camp with a tree-throw pit dwelling; partly open woodland with meadow clearings; aurochs bones.

attested: Spring at c. 11 C, pit dwelling, aurochs, flints (sto-wp-blickmead)
Partly open woodland and meadow-like clearings (sto-soton-blickmead2022)
inferred: Continuous occupation

features.name: Roman-period activity in the landscape
features.latLonSource: scattered; Cuckoo Stone building at sto-wp-cuckoo coordinates

dates.dateNote: Roman Britain 43-410 CE (general). Evidence is sparse.

appearanceByPeriod.show: Little beyond arable colluviation across the downs; a small rectangular building (probable shrine) near the Cuckoo Stone; coins and pottery at the stones; a large Roman graveyard near the Archer grave, and a Romano-British settlement overlooking the Avon (Wikipedia: 'likely').

attested: Roman building and coins at the Cuckoo Stone (sto-wp-cuckoo)
Late 4th c. coins, Roman pottery at Stonehenge (sto-wp-stonehenge)
Colluviation linked to arable continued through Roman times (sto-french2012)
inferred: Large Romano-British settlement at Amesbury (sto-wp-amesbury says likely)
unknown: Roads in the immediate WHS (none found in fetched sources)
Roman activity at Durrington Walls (not found)

dates.dateNote: A decapitated man (28-32) died 600-690 CE; excavated within the stone circles (sto-wp-stonehenge). A 5th-century Anglo-Saxon disc brooch at a Blick Mead spring (search snippet only; not used).

features.name: Amesbury Abbey / Priory (Benedictine, then Fontevraud)
features.latLonSource: sto-wp-amesburyabbey (modern house site; medieval priory is nearby, exact location not given)

dates.dateNote: Benedictine abbey founded c. 979 by Queen Ælfthryth; dissolved by Henry II in 1177 and refounded as a Fontevraud priory; dissolved 1540 per sto-wp-amesbury (the abbey article gives no date; brief says 1539). Buildings demolished; the parish church survived. The Crown granted the estate to Edward Seymour, Earl of Hertford, from the 1540s; Seymours held it until 1675 (sto-wp-amesbury). The mansion by Hopper (1834-40) and the 1661 mansion are later than 1625.

appearanceByPeriod.show: Benedictine nunnery beside the church; stone and timber claustral buildings (form unknown).
Fontevraud priory, a large religious house by the Avon with the parish church (St Mary and St Melor); Henry III and Eleanor of Provence stayed.
Priory buildings demolished; the estate under the Seymour/Hertford family; manor house of the Seymours (form not retrieved).

attested: 979 foundation, 1177 refoundation (sto-wp-amesburyabbey, sto-wp-amesbury)
Priory dissolved c. 1540; estate to Seymour (sto-wp-amesbury)
inferred: Layout

features.name: Amesbury town and medieval landscape
features.latLonSource: same as Amesbury Abbey (sto-wp-amesburyabbey), nearby

dates.dateNote: Domesday (1086): 111 households, eight mills (sto-wp-amesbury). Saxon settlement from the 7th century (a monastery perhaps earlier, weak).

appearanceByPeriod.show: Saxon village on the Avon, mills.

Small town on the Avon crossing of the London-Exeter road (Wikipedia: 'important river crossing'), abbey/priory adjoining; open fields on the downs; Coneybury ridge-and-furrow shows cultivation. Sheep downland: not documented in fetched sources.

attested: Domesday figures (sto-wp-amesbury)
Ridge and furrow over Coneybury (sto-wp-coneybury)
inferred: Sheep-corn husbandry on the downs (general chalkland pattern; no fetched source)

features.name: River Avon (Wiltshire Avon)
features.latLonSource: flows through Durrington and Amesbury (sto-wp-avon); local course held by other researchers

dates.dateNote: Always present. Floodplain cover: alder-hazel carr and sedges fringing the Avon through the Neolithic and Bronze Age; colluviation and channel sedimentation increased with clearance c. 800-500 BCE (sto-french2012).

appearanceByPeriod.show: Narrow clear chalk-fed river with alder-hazel carr and sedge fringe; shallow wet floodplain.
Sediment-laden at times, floodplain open with sedge fringe; water meadows are medieval (not sourced).

attested: Course Upavon to Durrington to Amesbury to Salisbury (sto-wp-avon)
Episodic increases in channel sedimentation with clearance (sto-french2012)
inferred: Chalk-stream character (Wikipedia carries only a category tag)
